clinicalPearls: Chronic pelvic pain, pressure or discomfort perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary urgency or frequency, in the absence of infection or another identifiable cause.
Predominantly affects women and frequently coexists with other central sensitivity and functional syndromes such as fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome and vulvodynia.
Pain characteristically worsens as the bladder fills and is transiently relieved by voiding.
Two clinically important phenotypes exist: Hunner lesion (classic, ulcerative) disease and non-Hunner disease, which require different treatment strategies.
Diagnosis is largely clinical and one of exclusion; cystoscopy is used mainly to identify Hunner lesions and to exclude other pathology.

Management is stepwise and multimodal, spanning behavioural and dietary measures, oral agents, intravesical therapy, hydrodistension, lesion-directed treatment, neuromodulation and, rarely, reconstructive surgery.
Hunner lesions can be treated directly with fulguration or intralesional steroid, often giving marked symptom relief.
A defective glycosaminoglycan layer and mast cell activation are central to the leading pathophysiological model.
reference.pathophysiology: The pathogenesis is multifactorial and incompletely understood. A leading model centres on a defective urothelial glycosaminoglycan layer and impaired urothelial barrier, allowing urinary solutes such as potassium to penetrate the urothelium, depolarise sensory afferents and trigger mast cell activation. Mast cell degranulation releases histamine and other mediators, producing neurogenic inflammation, upregulation of sensory nerves and, over time, central sensitisation that amplifies pain and accounts for the overlap with other chronic pain syndromes. An antiproliferative factor produced by the urothelium is thought to impair epithelial repair and perpetuate barrier dysfunction. Hunner lesion disease appears to represent a distinct inflammatory phenotype, with a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells and features suggesting an autoimmune contribution, whereas non-Hunner disease shows less pronounced inflammatory change.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial cystitis, including infection with fastidious organisms
Carcinoma in situ of the bladder
Radiation or chemical (for example cyclophosphamide) cystitis
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and urine culture to exclude infection
Urine cytology to exclude malignancy, particularly carcinoma in situ
Cystoscopy, often with hydrodistension under anaesthesia, to identify Hunner lesions and glomerulations
Bladder biopsy where malignancy or the degree of inflammation needs assessment
Post-void residual measurement and pelvic ultrasound
redFlags: Visible haematuria, which mandates exclusion of bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ
New irritative symptoms in an older patient or a smoker, raising malignancy risk
Sterile pyuria, prompting consideration of tuberculosis or malignancy
A positive urine culture indicating infection rather than the syndrome
Rapidly progressive symptoms or a palpable pelvic mass
reference.prognosis: IC/BPS is a chronic, relapsing and remitting condition in which symptom control rather than cure is the usual goal, and it can substantially impair quality of life. Hunner lesion disease often responds well to lesion-directed therapy, though symptoms may recur.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating culture-negative urinary tract infections with antibiotics
Missing Hunner lesions and therefore withholding phenotype-specific therapy
Overlooking bladder carcinoma in situ, which can mimic the syndrome
Reliance on the discredited potassium sensitivity test
Neglecting pelvic floor dysfunction and central pain contributors
references: Urology society guidance on interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome
European urology guidance on chronic pelvic pain
